# Lab 13.11: AI.KEY_DRIVERS & AI.CAUSAL_EFFECT

## What We Are Going to Do
Find which segments drove a jump in bike trips with AI.KEY_DRIVERS, then estimate the effect of the change with AI.CAUSAL_EFFECT through conversational analytics.

## Steps

1. **[SQL] Build a before/after table.**


<div style="margin:18px 0;border:1px solid #334155;border-radius:8px;overflow:hidden;">
<div style="background:#243244;color:#DBEAFE;padding:7px 12px;font-family:Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif;font-size:12px;font-weight:700;">
CODE • SQL
</div>
<pre style="margin:0;background:#111827;color:#F3F4F6;padding:16px;overflow-x:auto;white-space:pre;font-family:Consolas,'Cascadia Code',monospace;font-size:14px;line-height:1.55;"><code><span style="color:#F3F4F6;">CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE lab13.bike_change AS
SELECT
  subscriber_type, bike_type, start_station_name,
  DATE(start_time) &gt;= '2018-02-01' AS is_after,
  COUNT(*) AS trips
FROM `bigquery-public-data.austin_bikeshare.bikeshare_trips`
WHERE DATE(start_time) BETWEEN '2018-01-01' AND '2018-02-28'
GROUP BY 1, 2, 3, 4;</span>
</code></pre>
</div>


2. **[SQL] Find the key drivers.**


<div style="margin:18px 0;border:1px solid #334155;border-radius:8px;overflow:hidden;">
<div style="background:#243244;color:#DBEAFE;padding:7px 12px;font-family:Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif;font-size:12px;font-weight:700;">
CODE • SQL
</div>
<pre style="margin:0;background:#111827;color:#F3F4F6;padding:16px;overflow-x:auto;white-space:pre;font-family:Consolas,'Cascadia Code',monospace;font-size:14px;line-height:1.55;"><code><span style="color:#F3F4F6;">SELECT *
FROM AI.KEY_DRIVERS(
  TABLE lab13.bike_change,
  metric_col =&gt; 'trips',
  dimension_cols =&gt; ['subscriber_type', 'bike_type', 'start_station_name'],
  interest_label_col =&gt; 'is_after'
)
LIMIT 10;</span>
</code></pre>
</div>


   Each row is a segment (a combination of dimension values) that changed much more than expected.

3. **[Console] Measure the causal effect with conversational analytics.** Open **Agents → Conversational analytics**, add `bigquery-public-data.austin_bikeshare.bikeshare_trips` as a source and ask:

   *"Daily trips jumped in February 2018 when UT students got free memberships. Use AI.CAUSAL_EFFECT to estimate how many extra trips the programme caused compared with the expected baseline."*

   Check the generated SQL and the result: extra trips, percentage lift and probability of a real effect.

4. **[CLI] Run the key-drivers query from bq.**


<div style="margin:18px 0;border:1px solid #334155;border-radius:8px;overflow:hidden;">
<div style="background:#243244;color:#DBEAFE;padding:7px 12px;font-family:Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif;font-size:12px;font-weight:700;">
CODE • BASH
</div>
<pre style="margin:0;background:#111827;color:#F3F4F6;padding:16px;overflow-x:auto;white-space:pre;font-family:Consolas,'Cascadia Code',monospace;font-size:14px;line-height:1.55;"><code><span style="color:#F3F4F6;">bq query --use_legacy_sql=false \
"SELECT * FROM AI.KEY_DRIVERS(TABLE lab13.bike_change, metric_col =&gt; 'trips',
  dimension_cols =&gt; ['subscriber_type','bike_type'], interest_label_col =&gt; 'is_after') LIMIT 5"</span>
</code></pre>
</div>


## Expected Result

| Thing | Reality |
|---|---|
| Key drivers | Segments behind the change (for example UT students) |
| Max dimensions | 12 |
| Causal effect | Lift above a forecasted baseline |
| Related functions | ML.DETECT_CHANGE_POINTS, ML.CORRELATION, ML.TREND |
